context.en-US: Cancer is characterized by Hallmarks of Cancer. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The Hallmarks of Cancer are the enabling biological capabilities acquired during tumorigenesis, including sustained proliferation, evasion of death, and metastasis. The directionality runs from Hallmarks of Cancer toward Cancer, so Hallmarks of Cancer is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Together these facts situate the relationship within the broader architecture of cancer biology, clarifying how the two entities connect as part of the hallmark or taxonomic framework.

Avermectin B1a is the natural macrocyclic-lactone precursor of ivermectin (22,23-dihydroavermectin B1a), the semi-synthetic lead derivative developed for human and veterinary medicine.
Ivermectin is the 22,23-dihydro derivative of avermectin B1a, produced by chemical reduction of the natural avermectin fermentation product.
Avermectins are 16-membered macrocyclic lactones biosynthesized by the soil actinomycete Streptomyces avermectinius (formerly S. avermitilis).
Avermectins are allosteric potentiators/agonists of invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels (GluCls); Cl- influx hyperpolarizes and paralyzes parasites.
Avermectins also potentiate invertebrate GABA-gated chloride channels; vertebrate GABA_A receptors require roughly 100-fold higher concentrations, underpinning selective safety.
Avermectin's derivative ivermectin is under active preclinical investigation for anticancer repositioning (Wnt/beta-catenin, AKT/mTOR and PAK1 inhibition; apoptosis; multidrug-resistance reversal).
Ivermectin is a positive allosteric modulator/agonist of invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels, causing sustained Cl- influx and parasite paralysis.
Humans and other vertebrates lack glutamate-gated chloride channels, which underpins the selective safety of avermectin/ivermectin at therapeutic doses.
Activation of GluCls in nematodes and arthropods drives Cl- influx, membrane hyperpolarization, flaccid paralysis and death.
Satoshi Omura performed the soil-microbe screening that isolated Streptomyces avermectinius at the Kitasato Institute, Tokyo.
Avermectin was discovered from a soil actinomycete isolated at the Kitasato Institute; the lead strain yielded the ivermectin precursor.
The avermectin-producing strain Streptomyces avermectinius was isolated from Japanese soil at the Kitasato Institute.
Omura isolated and cultured Streptomyces avermectinius from Japanese soil, the sole known natural source of avermectins.

Leukemia is a clonal hematologic malignancy arising from abnormal hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells.
Leukemic clones derive from transformed hematopoietic stem or progenitor cells.
Ivermectin preferentially kills leukemia cells at low concentrations while sparing normal hematopoietic cells in preclinical screens (Tang et al., 2020; PMID 32971268).
Benzimidazole anthelmintics including fenbendazole show preclinical anticancer activity across leukemic models via microtubule disruption.
Mebendazole exerts preclinical antileukemic effects through tubulin depolymerization and mitotic arrest.
Leukemia is treated with cytotoxic chemotherapy and, in selected cases, targeted agents; ivermectin's activity remains preclinical.
Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the bile-duct epithelium (adenocarcinoma).
First-line systemic therapy is gemcitabine plus cisplatin; options remain limited and prognosis poor.
Ivermectin suppresses cholangiocarcinoma cell proliferation and migration in preclinical models.
Fenbendazole is under preclinical investigation for cholangiocarcinoma as part of the repurposed anthelmintic anticancer cluster.
Mebendazole shows preclinical antiproliferative activity in cholangiocarcinoma via microtubule interference.
Cholangiocarcinoma harbors cancer stem-like cells that drive recurrence and chemoresistance.
Mebendazole is a benzimidazole anthelmintic in the same class as fenbendazole and albendazole.
Mebendazole binds the colchicine site of beta-tubulin, inhibiting microtubule polymerization (Sasaki et al., Mol Cancer Ther 2002).
By blocking tubulin polymerization, mebendazole disrupts the mitotic spindle, causing G2/M arrest and apoptosis.
Mebendazole elicits potent antitumor effects in vitro and in vivo across multiple cancers (Mukhopadhyay et al., Clin Cancer Res 2002).
Mebendazole induces mitotic arrest and apoptosis in cancer cells via microtubule depolymerization.
Mebendazole and fenbendazole are structurally related benzimidazole anthelmintics with overlapping anticancer mechanisms.
